title: History of Weiqi
audience: readers who have followed the structural lessons and want institutional and historical context for weiqi
learningGoal: trace how weiqi spread from its origins in China across East Asia and into global play while keeping its core rules intact

steps.title: Reading 1
steps.text: Weiqi's history is a long record of transmission and institutional refinement: a game that began in China, spread across East Asia, and later became a global competitive and educational tradition.

steps.title: Reading 2
steps.text: One game, three names. The same game is commonly called weiqi in Chinese, baduk in Korean, and go in Japanese-derived English usage. Those names mark more than translation — they show the route by which the game moved across linguistic and institutional settings while keeping a recognizable rules core.

steps.title: Reading 3
steps.text: Origins in China. The game originated in China more than two millennia ago, and some accounts place it much earlier. Early Chinese traditions treated it not only as recreation but as a cultivated art associated with scholarly accomplishment. What matters historically is durability: weiqi kept the same basic logic of placement, enclosure, and capture across centuries even as rule explanations, board conventions, and social settings changed.

steps.title: Reading 4
steps.text: Transmission across East Asia. Weiqi spread from China to Korea and Japan, where it developed strong local traditions and institutions. Japanese professional houses later played a major role in codifying teaching lineages, recording famous games, and circulating the name go beyond Japan. This transmission changed how the game was taught and organized, but not its basic identity: the core mechanics remained territorial placement, capture, and shape judgment. The major historical shifts were institutional and cultural rather than mechanical.

steps.title: Reading 5
steps.text: Modern international play. In the twentieth century, weiqi expanded far beyond East Asia through national associations, translated teaching materials, and international federations. That growth made rank systems, tournament rules, and teaching methods more legible to new players outside the game's older centers. Organizations outside East Asia often present handicap play as a normal and valuable part of the game, not as a lesser version of it — an emphasis that helped weiqi travel as both a competitive discipline and a teachable social practice.

steps.title: Exercise 1
steps.prompt: What does the existence of the names weiqi, baduk, and go show about the game's history?
steps.answer: It shows that the game spread across different linguistic and institutional settings while preserving a recognizable core structure.

steps.title: Exercise 2
steps.prompt: What changed most as weiqi spread internationally: its basic mechanics or its institutions of teaching and competition?
steps.answer: Its institutions changed more than its basic mechanics. The game kept the same territorial placement logic while different regions developed their own teaching systems, organizations, and naming traditions.
